title: Secrets Management
subtitle: Watch a database password go from a leaked file to a short-lived credential that a vault hands out and then revokes.
learn: Why secrets in source code, images, and env files keep leaking
How a vault issues and audits secrets instead of storing copies everywhere
How short-lived, dynamic credentials shrink the damage of a leak
How rotation works without downtime, using overlapping validity
How workload identity removes the first secret needed to reach the vault

steps.title: Where does the password live?
steps.body: The payments service must log in to the orders database, so it needs a credential: a secret. Whatever holds that secret becomes as sensitive as the database itself. The question is where to keep it so the service can read it but nobody else can, and so that a leak is survivable.
steps.idea: A secret is only as safe as the least-protected place a copy of it sits.
steps.caption: The service needs a credential to reach the database.

steps.title: Secrets in code get cloned
steps.body: The easy answer is to commit the password to the repo or bake it into the container image. Now every developer laptop, CI runner, fork, and image registry holds a copy, and git history keeps it even after you delete the line. Bots scan public repos for keys within minutes, and a private repo leak is just a stolen laptop away. The password is rarely changed, so it stays valid for a year or more (shown as 525,600 minutes).
steps.idea: Code and images are copied freely by design, so a secret inside them is copied freely too.
steps.caption: The secret rides along with every copy of the repo.

steps.title: Env files only move the problem
steps.body: Env vars and .env files keep the secret out of git, which is a real improvement. But the file still gets pasted into chat, copied to each server, printed by crash dumps and debug endpoints, and inherited by every child process. It is still one long-lived static value with no record of who read it, and changing it means editing every place it was copied.
steps.idea: Env vars are a delivery mechanism, not a store: no access control, no audit, no expiry.
steps.caption: Still a static password, now scattered across hosts.

steps.title: Workload identity: prove who you are
steps.body: A vault would hold the secret in one place, but the service must then authenticate to it, which risks a first-secret problem. Workload identity solves this. The platform (Kubernetes, a cloud provider, SPIFFE) vouches for the running workload and issues it a signed token, valid for around ten minutes, with no password stored anywhere.
steps.idea: Let the platform attest who the workload is, so no bootstrap secret has to be shipped with it.
steps.caption: The platform issues a short-lived identity token.

steps.title: The vault checks the token, then lends
steps.body: The service presents its token to the vault. The vault verifies the signature against the identity provider, looks up a policy (payments may read only the orders-db path), and answers. Every read is written to an audit log: who, what, when. Secrets are stored encrypted, so the vault becomes the one place to protect, monitor, and rate-limit.
steps.idea: A vault centralizes storage, policy, and audit, so access is a decision rather than a copy.
steps.caption: Identity is verified and policy allows one path.

steps.title: Dynamic credentials with a TTL
steps.body: Even better, the vault does not hand out a stored password. It connects to the database, creates a brand-new user with only the needed grants, and returns it with a one-hour lease. Each service instance gets its own unique login, so logs show exactly which instance did what. Nothing static exists to steal from a repo.
steps.idea: Short-lived, per-instance credentials turn a permanent secret into a disposable one.
steps.caption: Vault creates a one-hour database user on demand.

steps.title: Rotation without downtime
steps.body: Some systems cannot mint users on demand, such as a third-party API key or a legacy database, so you rotate the secret on a schedule, often every 30 to 90 days. The safe pattern is overlap: create the new secret, keep the old one valid for a grace period, let services pick up the new one, then retire the old. A flip-the-switch rotation causes an outage.
steps.idea: Rotate by overlapping old and new, so readers can switch over before the old value dies.
steps.caption: Vault rotates the credential while both stay valid.

steps.title: A leaked log line
steps.body: Suppose a debug log accidentally prints the live database credential and an attacker finds it. With a static password they would own the database indefinitely. Here they can use it only until the lease ends, at most an hour. Network rules and a database user limited to a few tables narrow the damage further.
steps.idea: Lifetime and scope bound the damage; you cannot always prevent a leak, but you can cap it.
steps.caption: Stolen credential works, but only inside its TTL.

steps.title: Revoke on detection
steps.body: Your alerting spots a login from an unfamiliar address. An operator revokes the lease in the vault, which drops that database user within seconds. Contrast this with a static shared password: you would have to rotate it and redeploy every consumer at once. Revocation by lease ID is cheap precisely because credentials were issued individually. Assume it takes about five minutes to notice the login and decide to revoke; the revoke itself takes seconds.
steps.idea: Per-lease issuance makes revocation surgical instead of a company-wide fire drill.
steps.caption: The vault drops the stolen user; attacker is locked out.

steps.title: Few copies, short lives
steps.body: Keep secrets out of code, images, and env files. Let the platform prove who the workload is, let a vault decide and log who may read what, and prefer dynamic credentials that expire on their own. Where a secret must be static, rotate it with an overlap. The aim is not a perfect secret but a leak that costs minutes, not months.
steps.idea: Identity instead of bootstrap secrets, vault instead of copies, expiry instead of hope.
steps.caption: Identity, vault, short leases, fast revoke.

quiz.q: A developer deletes a committed database password in the next commit and pushes. Is the secret safe?
options: Yes, the file no longer contains it
Yes, if the repo is private
No, it remains in git history and any clone, so it must be rotated
Only if the commit is squashed in CI
quiz.why: Git keeps history and clones copy it. Once a secret has been committed, treat it as exposed and rotate it; removing the line does not.

quiz.q: Why is workload identity better than giving each service a vault token stored in its config?
options: Tokens in config are slower to validate
The config token is itself a long-lived secret that must be delivered and protected
Vaults cannot validate config tokens
Workload identity encrypts the database traffic
quiz.why: A stored vault token just recreates the original problem one level up. Platform-attested identity avoids shipping any bootstrap secret.

quiz.q: An attacker steals a dynamic database credential with a 1-hour lease from a log file. Which statement is most accurate?
options: They have access forever, same as a static password
They have access until the lease expires or is revoked, limited to that user's grants
The credential is useless the moment it is logged
They can ask the vault to renew it
quiz.why: A bounded TTL and narrow grants cap the damage, and revoking the lease ends access early. Renewal requires the service's own identity, which the attacker lacks.

quiz.q: You must rotate an API key used by 30 running instances with zero downtime. What is the safest approach?
options: Replace the key everywhere at the same instant
Stop the service, change the key, restart
Create the new key, keep the old valid briefly, let instances switch, then retire the old key
Rotate only when an incident occurs
quiz.why: Overlapping validity lets instances pick up the new value at different times without failed requests; an instant flip guarantees some callers hold a dead key.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest argument for a vault over an encrypted .env file kept in the repo?
options: Vaults use a stronger cipher
It adds per-read policy, audit logs, expiry, and revocation
It avoids needing any authentication
It makes secrets smaller
quiz.why: The encrypted file still needs a decryption key, offers no per-reader audit, and cannot expire or revoke. Control and visibility, not cipher strength, are the vault's value.

cheatsheet.def: Any value that grants access if known: passwords, API keys, private keys, tokens, connection strings.
A service that stores secrets encrypted, enforces per-identity policy, and logs every read. Examples: HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager.
A credential minted on demand for one client with a TTL, then deleted automatically. No stored password to leak.
The time a credential is valid. Short leases (minutes to hours) limit leak damage; leases can be renewed or revoked.
Replacing a secret on a schedule or after exposure. Use overlap, with old and new valid together, to avoid downtime.
A platform-issued, signed identity for a running workload (Kubernetes service account token, cloud IAM role, SPIFFE ID). Removes the bootstrap secret.
What an attacker can reach with one stolen secret. Shrink it with least-privilege grants, per-service credentials, and expiry.
Automated checks in pre-commit hooks and CI that block commits containing keys. A safety net, not a replacement for a vault.
